title: Europe, Asia and the Americas Compared
bigQuestion: How can we compare whole societies fairly without flattening the people who live in them?

story.title: Eighteen in Three Places
story.kicker: Three exchange students at a Chicago-area high school discover that turning eighteen means different things at home.
paragraphs: It is lunch in the cafeteria of a high school outside Chicago. Three exchange students share a table this year. Lena is from Leipzig, in eastern Germany. Haruto is from Osaka, in Japan. Sofía is from Guadalajara, in western Mexico. A teacher has asked them one question for a class project: what does your family expect of you at eighteen?

Lena answers first. At eighteen she can vote, sign contracts and move out, and many of her friends will. Her older brother chose a three-year apprenticeship as an electrician instead of university. He is paid while he trains, and her parents call that a smart path. What they expect most, Lena says, is that she stands on her own feet.

Haruto laughs. In Japan the legal age of adulthood dropped from twenty to eighteen in 2022, but his parents still talk about the coming-of-age ceremony. What they expect most is effort on the university entrance exams. His grandmother lives with his family, and he is expected to help care for her. He says the word for it is responsibility, not obedience.

Sofía says her family threw her a big quinceañera at fifteen, with cousins from three states. At eighteen she can vote in Mexico too. But no one expects her to move out soon. Many young adults she knows live at home until they marry or find steady work. What her family expects most, she says, is that she stays close and helps the family move forward together.

Then all three notice something. Each has a friend at home whose family is nothing like theirs. Lena has a friend who lives with her grandmother. Haruto has a cousin who skipped university to start a business. Sofía has a friend who moved alone to Mexico City at seventeen. Their teacher smiles. That, she says, is the first rule of comparing societies.
story.think: What patterns did the three students notice, and why do their friends at home matter when we compare whole countries?

lessons.title: Family Across Three Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Germany, Japan and Mexico all value family, but they differ in household size, living arrangements and what adult children owe their parents.
reading: Picture three dinner tables. In a German apartment, two parents and one teenager eat together. In a Japanese home, a grandmother sits with her son, his wife and their child. In a Mexican house, aunts, cousins and grandparents drop by on Sunday. None of these scenes is the whole story of a country. But each reflects a real pattern that census data show.

A *household* is the group of people who live under one roof. German households are small on average, and many adults live alone, especially in big cities. Japan has long had a tradition of the *extended family*, where three generations share a home. That pattern has shrunk as young people move to cities, yet many older Japanese still live with or near a grown child. Mexican households are larger on average, and relatives often live close by and share child care.

Duties inside families differ too. In Japan, caring for aging parents has been treated as a key duty, often falling on a daughter or daughter-in-law. In Mexico, *familismo* describes a strong sense of loyalty and mutual help among relatives. In Germany, the state pays for more of the care of the old and the young, so families lean less on each other for money. Supporters of each pattern point to its strengths, and critics point to the strain on some members, often women.

words.d: the group of people who live together under one roof
a family that includes grandparents, aunts, uncles or cousins, not just parents and children
a Spanish term for strong loyalty, closeness and mutual help among relatives

look.title: Three Sunday Afternoons
look.text: Scene A: a woman in Hamburg video-calls her mother, then goes hiking with friends. Scene B: a man in Nagoya drives his father to a doctor, then eats lunch with him. Scene C: a teenager in Puebla helps her aunt cook for twelve relatives. Each scene is common in its country, and each also happens in the other two countries.
look.prompt: Which scene fits the pattern described for each country, and what would you need to know before saying a scene is typical?

check.q: What does the term household mean?
choices: All the relatives a person has anywhere
The group of people who live together under one roof
A family that owns its own home
check.why: A household is defined by living together, not by how many relatives someone has.

check.q: Which country in the reading has larger average households with relatives often sharing child care?
check.why: The reading says Mexican households are larger on average and relatives often share child care.

check.q: Why do German families lean less on each other for money, according to the reading?
choices: The state pays for more care of the old and the young
German law forbids living with parents
German families have no older members
Most Germans live in the countryside
check.why: The reading links the difference to the state paying for more care, not to a lack of family feeling.

lessons.title: Class and Getting Ahead
lessons.mainIdea: Each society offers different main roads to a good job: apprenticeships in Germany, exam-based schooling in Japan, and a mix of formal and informal work in Mexico.
reading: Lena's brother trains as an electrician. Three days a week he works at a company, and two days he studies at a vocational school. This is Germany's *dual system* of training. A large share of young Germans choose it, and skilled trades carry real respect. Supporters say it gives many young people a steady path without a university degree. Critics say students are sorted into tracks too early, at around age ten in many states, which can lock in class differences.

In Japan, the main road runs through schools and exams. Getting into a well-known university has long led to jobs at large companies. Many of those jobs once promised *lifetime employment*, meaning a worker could stay with one firm until retirement. That promise has weakened since the 1990s. Today almost four in ten Japanese workers hold part-time or temporary jobs, with lower pay and less security.

In Mexico, a large share of people work in the *informal economy*: street vendors, small family shops and day laborers who pay no payroll taxes and get no official benefits. Mexico's statistics agency, INEGI, counts a little over half of workers this way. Some informal businesses thrive, and some owners prefer the freedom. But informal workers often lack health coverage and pensions, which makes moving up harder. Economists debate whether lower taxes, easier rules or stronger enforcement would help most.

words.d: Germany's training model that combines paid work at a company with classes at a vocational school
a practice at some large Japanese firms of keeping workers from school until retirement
work that is not registered with the government, so it pays no payroll taxes and gets no official benefits
the movement of people up or down between classes during their lives or across generations

look.title: Three Paths at Nineteen
look.text: Jonas in Stuttgart is in the second year of a paid apprenticeship as a car mechanic. Aiko in Sendai is studying for a second try at a university entrance exam. Diego in Monterrey sells phone cases from a stall his uncle runs, and takes night classes in accounting.
look.prompt: For each young person, name the road to a job described in the reading, and one thing that could help or block their social mobility.

check.q: What is Germany's dual system?
choices: Training that combines paid company work with vocational school classes
A school day split between two languages
A rule that everyone attends university twice
check.why: The dual system pairs work at a company with classes at a vocational school.

check.q: What does the reading say has happened to lifetime employment in Japan?
choices: It became required by law in 2022
It has weakened since the 1990s, and many workers now hold part-time or temporary jobs
It spread to all small businesses
check.why: The reading says the promise weakened after the 1990s and almost four in ten workers now hold non-regular jobs.

check.q: Which worker is part of the informal economy?
choices: A street vendor who pays no payroll taxes and gets no official benefits
A teacher at a public school
An apprentice registered with a German company
A bank clerk with a pension plan
check.why: Informal work is not registered with the government, so it carries no payroll taxes or official benefits.

lessons.title: How Each Country Governs
lessons.mainIdea: Germany, Japan and Mexico are all democracies, but they organize power differently: a federal parliamentary system, a parliamentary monarchy and a federal presidential republic.
reading: After defeat in World War II, both Germany and Japan wrote new constitutions. West Germany adopted its *Basic Law* in 1949, and it became the constitution of all Germany at reunification in 1990. Germany is a federal republic of sixteen states. Voters elect the Bundestag, the national parliament, and it chooses the chancellor, who leads the government. The Basic Law opens by protecting human dignity, a direct answer to the crimes of the Nazi years.

Japan's constitution took effect in 1947. It keeps the emperor, but only as a symbol of the state with no power to govern. This is a *constitutional monarchy*. Voters elect the Diet, the two-house parliament, and the Diet chooses the prime minister. One party, the Liberal Democratic Party, has led Japan for most years since 1955. Supporters see stability; critics see too little competition.

Mexico's constitution dates from 1917, after the Mexican Revolution. Mexico is a federal republic with a *presidential system*: voters elect the president directly, separate from Congress. A president serves one six-year term and can never run again, a rule born from anger at long-ruling leaders. For most of the twentieth century one party, the PRI, won every presidential election. In 2000 a candidate from another party won, and Mexico's elections became openly competitive.

words.d: Germany's constitution, adopted in 1949 and extended to the whole country in 1990
a system with a king, queen or emperor whose powers are limited or only symbolic, while elected leaders govern
a government in which voters elect the president separately from the legislature
a system that divides power between a national government and state or regional governments

look.title: The First Line of Germany's Constitution
look.text: Human dignity cannot be violated. Every part of the state's power has a duty to respect it and protect it.
look.cite: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany, Article 1, 1949 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why might a country that had just lived through the Nazi years choose to begin its constitution with this idea?

check.q: In which country do voters elect the president directly for a single six-year term?
check.why: Mexico's presidential system limits the president to one six-year term.

check.q: What role does Japan's emperor have under the 1947 constitution?
choices: He writes the laws with the Diet
He is a symbol of the state with no power to govern
check.why: Japan is a constitutional monarchy in which the emperor is only a symbol.

check.q: Who chooses Germany's chancellor?
choices: The president of the European Union
check.why: In Germany's parliamentary system the Bundestag elects the chancellor.

lessons.title: Culture in Daily Life
lessons.mainIdea: Festivals, food and shared customs show what a culture honors, and each one changes over time as people remake it.
reading: In early November, families across Mexico build *ofrendas*, home altars with marigolds, photographs, candles and a loved one's favorite foods. This is the Day of the Dead. It honors ancestors with joy as well as grief. UNESCO added it to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage in 2008. In Chicago, the National Museum of Mexican Art in the Pilsen neighborhood hosts a large Day of the Dead exhibition each year.

In Japan, many families travel home in summer for Obon, when ancestors' spirits are welcomed back with lanterns and dances. In Germany, towns fill with Christmas markets in December, with wooden stalls, mulled drinks and carols. Each of these is a *tradition*, a custom handed down across generations. Notice that all three honor family and memory, even though they look very different.

Traditions are not frozen. Many Japanese couples now hold Western-style wedding ceremonies. German Christmas markets draw tourists who are not Christian. The Day of the Dead grew more widely known after films and parades spread its images. Scholars call this *cultural change*. Some people welcome it as living culture; others worry that meaning is lost when customs become commercial.

words.d: home altars built for the Day of the Dead, with photos, flowers, candles and food for loved ones who have died
a custom or belief handed down from one generation to the next
the way customs, beliefs and ways of life shift over time as people borrow, adapt or drop them

look.title: Three Festivals, One Thread
look.text: Mexico: marigold petals lead from the door to an altar with a grandfather's photo. Japan: a family lights a small fire at the gate to guide ancestors home for Obon. Germany: a family visits a Christmas market together, the way grandparents did decades ago.
look.prompt: What value do these three scenes share, and how does each tradition express it in its own way?

check.q: What is an ofrenda?
choices: A home altar for the Day of the Dead
check.why: Ofrendas are altars with photos, flowers and food honoring loved ones who have died.

check.q: Which festival welcomes ancestors' spirits back home in summer?
check.why: Obon is the Japanese summer festival that welcomes ancestors home.

check.q: According to the reading, what do some people worry about when traditions change?
choices: That no one will travel home
That meaning is lost when customs become commercial
That UNESCO will remove them from its list
check.why: The reading says some worry that commercial versions lose the meaning of the custom.

lessons.title: Welfare States Compared
lessons.mainIdea: A welfare state uses taxes to protect people against illness, old age and job loss, and countries differ sharply in how much they do and who pays.
reading: In the 1880s, German chancellor Otto von Bismarck created the world's first national social insurance: health insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884, and old-age pensions in 1889. Bismarck was a conservative. He hoped the programs would win workers away from socialist parties. His model still shapes Germany, where workers and employers pay into insurance funds. This is one type of *welfare state*, a government that protects people against life's major risks.

The Danish scholar Gøsta Esping-Andersen, in a famous 1990 book, sorted rich democracies into three types. Liberal welfare states, like the United States, offer more modest help and rely more on markets. Conservative welfare states, like Germany, tie benefits to work and family. Social democratic welfare states, like Sweden, offer broad benefits to everyone, paid for with high taxes. Japan borrowed from several models and also leans on large companies and families.

Mexico created its social security institute, the IMSS, in 1943 for workers in formal jobs. Because so many work informally, millions were left out. In 1997 Mexico launched Progresa, which paid poor families cash if their children attended school and had health checkups. It became a model copied in many countries. Supporters of big welfare states say they reduce poverty and fear. Critics say high *social spending* can slow growth, raise debt and weaken the habit of self-reliance. Economists still debate how large the trade-offs are.

words.d: a government that uses taxes to protect people against risks such as illness, old age, disability and job loss
programs that workers and employers pay into, which then pay benefits when someone is sick, old or out of work
the money a government spends on pensions, health care, family support and other social programs
a program that gives poor families money if they meet conditions such as keeping children in school

look.title: Public Social Spending
look.cite: OECD Social Expenditure Database (SOCX), early 2020s, rounded
look.prompt: About how many times more of its economy does Germany spend on social programs than Mexico, and what reasons from the reading might explain the gap?

check.q: Why did Bismarck, a conservative, create social insurance in the 1880s?
choices: To prepare Germany for a war with Japan
To obey a law passed by the European Union
To copy a program from Mexico
To win workers away from socialist parties
check.why: The reading says Bismarck hoped the programs would draw workers away from the socialists.

check.q: In Esping-Andersen's three types, which kind offers broad benefits to everyone, paid for with high taxes?
check.why: Social democratic welfare states, like Sweden, give broad benefits funded by high taxes.

check.q: What was Mexico's Progresa program?
choices: Cash for poor families if children attended school and had health checkups
A pension only for government workers
A training program for German apprentices
check.why: Progresa was a conditional cash transfer that tied payments to school and health visits.

lessons.title: Aging Societies
lessons.mainIdea: Japan and much of Europe are aging fast because people live longer and have fewer children, which strains pensions and care.
reading: In some rural Japanese towns, schools have closed for lack of children while clinics are full of older patients. Japan has one of the oldest populations in the world. About three in ten Japanese people are 65 or older. The average woman in Japan has about 1.2 children in her lifetime. A population needs about 2.1 to replace itself over time. This number is called the *replacement rate*.

The *fertility rate* is the average number of children a woman has. It has dropped below the replacement rate across Europe and East Asia. South Korea's rate fell below 1.0, the lowest in the world. Germany's is about 1.4. Mexico's has fallen too, to below 2.0, but Mexico is still a much younger country, with a median age around thirty. Japan's median age is near fifty.

An aging society has fewer workers paying taxes for each retiree drawing a pension. This is measured by the *dependency ratio*. Countries respond in different ways. Germany has raised its retirement age and relies more on immigration. Japan has invested in robots for care work and accepted more foreign workers, though more cautiously. Some leaders favor paying families to have children; others favor immigration; others favor longer working lives. Each choice has supporters and critics.

words.d: the average number of children born to a woman over her lifetime
the fertility rate, about 2.1, at which a population replaces itself without immigration
the number of children and older people compared with the number of working-age people
the age that splits a population in half: half are older and half are younger

look.title: Share of People Aged 65 and Older
look.cite: World Bank, World Development Indicators, from UN population data, about 2023, rounded
look.prompt: Which country has more than three times Mexico's share of older people, and what might that mean for its workers and pensions?

check.q: What is the replacement rate?
choices: The age at which people retire
The fertility rate of about 2.1 at which a population replaces itself
The share of workers who are immigrants
The number of schools that close each year
check.why: The replacement rate is about 2.1 children per woman.

check.q: Which country in the reading is much younger, with a median age around thirty?
check.why: The reading gives Mexico a median age around thirty and Japan near fifty.

check.q: Why does an aging society strain pensions?
choices: There are fewer workers paying taxes for each retiree
Older people pay more taxes than workers
Pensions are illegal in aging countries
Robots cannot pay into insurance funds
check.why: The dependency ratio rises: fewer workers support each person drawing a pension.

lessons.title: The Move to Cities
lessons.mainIdea: Most people in all three countries now live in cities, and giant metro areas like Tokyo and Mexico City bring both opportunity and strain.
reading: Greater Tokyo is the largest metropolitan area on Earth, home to about 37 million people by UN estimates. Trains arrive every few minutes, and millions ride them daily. Greater Mexico City holds over 20 million people. It sits on an old lakebed, and heavy pumping of groundwater has made parts of the city sink. *Urbanization* is the growth in the share of people who live in cities.

People move to cities for jobs, schools and hospitals. In Mexico, large numbers moved from farms to cities during the twentieth century. Many built homes themselves on the edges of cities, in *informal settlements* that later gained roads, water and titles. Germany urbanized earlier, during the 1800s, and its people are spread across many mid-sized cities rather than one giant capital.

Cities bring strain too. Housing costs rise, commutes lengthen and air can grow dirty. At the same time, the countryside can empty out. Japan now has thousands of empty rural houses, called akiya. Planners argue over the fixes. Some want more public housing and transit; others want fewer building rules so the market can add homes faster. A *megacity* of over ten million people needs both good planning and room to grow.

words.d: the growth in the share of a population that lives in cities
neighborhoods built by residents without official permits, often on the edge of a growing city
a metropolitan area with more than ten million people

look.title: Share of People Living in Cities
look.cite: United Nations, World Urbanization Prospects: The 2018 Revision, rounded
look.prompt: All three countries are more urban than the world as a whole. Using the reading, give one reason Germany's share is lower than Japan's even though it urbanized earlier.

check.q: What is urbanization?
choices: The growth in the share of people who live in cities
The rule that cities cannot grow
check.why: Urbanization means a rising share of people living in cities.

check.q: Which is the largest metropolitan area on Earth, by UN estimates?
check.why: The reading names Greater Tokyo, at about 37 million people.

check.q: What are informal settlements?
choices: Neighborhoods built by residents without official permits
check.why: Informal settlements are built without permits, often on a city's edge, and may later gain services.

lessons.title: Religion and Tradition Today
lessons.mainIdea: Religion shapes all three societies, but in different ways: church membership in Germany, practice without membership in Japan, and strong Catholic faith in Mexico.
reading: Every December 12, millions of pilgrims travel to the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City. It is one of the most visited Catholic sites in the world. In Mexico's 2020 census, about 78 percent of people called themselves Catholic, and a growing share named Protestant churches or no religion. Faith shapes holidays, family events and many people's sense of what Mexico is.

In Germany, members of registered churches pay a *church tax*, collected by the state along with income tax. Leaving a church ends the tax, and many Germans have left. By the early 2020s, fewer than half of Germans belonged to the Catholic or Protestant church. Germany is also home to millions of Muslims, many from families that came from Turkey as workers from the 1960s on.

Japan looks different again. Most Japanese tell surveys they do not belong to a religion. Yet many visit a Shinto shrine at New Year and hold Buddhist funerals. Scholars say Japanese religion is often about *practice*, what people do, more than *belief*, what people say they believe. This is a reminder that a label like secular can mean different things in different places.

words.d: a tax that members of registered churches pay in Germany, collected by the state
what people do in religion, such as rituals, festivals and visits to holy places
what people hold to be true about God, gods or the meaning of life
not connected to religion, or not tied to religious authority

look.title: Two Ways to Measure Religion
look.text: Survey A asks: Do you belong to a religion? Survey B asks: In the past year, did you visit a shrine, temple or church, or take part in a religious ceremony? In Japan, many people answer no to Survey A and yes to Survey B.
look.prompt: Which survey question tells you more about religion in Japan, and why could the answer differ in Mexico or Germany?

check.q: About what share of Mexicans called themselves Catholic in the 2020 census?
check.why: The reading gives about 78 percent, from Mexico's 2020 census.

check.q: What happens when a German leaves a registered church?
choices: They stop paying the church tax
They lose the right to vote
They must pay a higher income tax
check.why: The church tax is paid by members, so leaving the church ends it.

check.q: What do scholars mean when they say Japanese religion is often about practice more than belief?
choices: Japanese people practice only one religion
Many people take part in rituals even if they do not claim a religion
check.why: Many Japanese visit shrines and hold Buddhist funerals while saying they have no religion.

lessons.title: What Each Society Values
lessons.mainIdea: The fairest way to learn what a society values is to listen to how its own people describe it, through surveys, writing and conversation.
reading: Since 1981, the World Values Survey has asked people in about one hundred countries the same questions. How important is family? Is it more important for a child to learn obedience or independence? How much do you trust people you do not know? The answers let researchers compare values without relying on outsiders' guesses.

Political scientists Ronald Inglehart and Christian Welzel used the survey to draw a well-known map. One line runs from *traditional values*, stressing religion, family and respect for authority, to secular-rational values. Another runs from survival values, stressing security, to *self-expression values*, stressing free choice. On that map, Japan and Germany rank high on secular-rational values, and Mexico ranks more traditional and high in reported happiness.

Such maps are useful but limited. A country average hides big differences between young and old, city and village, rich and poor. People also describe their values in their own words. Many Japanese speak of harmony and consideration for others. Many Mexicans speak of family and faith. Many Germans speak of order, fairness and reliability. Each of these is a *self-description*, and each is only part of the picture.

words.d: values that stress religion, family ties and respect for authority
values that stress free choice, tolerance and a voice in decisions
how a group of people describes its own values, in its own words

look.title: Reading a Survey Answer
look.text: Imagine a survey finds that 80 percent of people in one country say family is very important, and 60 percent in another country say the same. A student writes: People in the second country do not care about their families.
look.prompt: What is wrong with the student's conclusion, and how would you rewrite it so it matches what the numbers actually show?

check.q: Why do researchers use the World Values Survey to compare countries?
choices: It lists every law in each country
It asks people in many countries the same questions about their own values
It is written by tourists who visited each country
check.why: The survey asks people directly, so comparisons do not rest on outsiders' guesses.

check.q: On the Inglehart-Welzel map, what do self-expression values stress?
choices: Free choice, tolerance and a voice in decisions
check.why: Self-expression values are about free choice and having a voice.

check.q: What is one limit of a country average?
choices: It hides big differences between groups inside the country
It cannot be written as a number
It only counts people over sixty-five
check.why: An average hides differences between young and old, city and village, rich and poor.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Stereotypes
lessons.mainIdea: A fair comparison uses evidence about patterns, names its sources and remembers that individuals differ from the average.
reading: Think back to the three exchange students. Each described a real pattern at home. Each also had a friend whose life broke the pattern. A *stereotype* is a fixed, oversimplified idea that all members of a group are alike. It turns a pattern into a rule and a rule into a judgment about people. Stereotypes can be negative or seemingly positive, and both kinds erase real people.

In a 2009 talk, the Nigerian novelist Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie warned about the danger of a single story. When we hear only one story about a people, she said, that story becomes the only thing we know about them. A careful comparison does the opposite. It asks, Compared with what? How many people? Measured by whom? It uses words like many, most and on average instead of all and always.

*Generalization* is not the enemy. Scholars need patterns to compare societies at all. The skill is to hold a pattern loosely. State what the evidence shows, name the source, and notice the exceptions. Also check your own *cultural lens*, the habits and values you grew up with that shape how you see others. What looks strange from outside often makes good sense to the people inside.

words.d: a fixed, oversimplified idea that all members of a group are the same
a statement about a pattern that holds for many members of a group, supported by evidence
the habits and values from your own upbringing that shape how you see other people

look.title: The Danger of a Single Story
look.text: Show a people as only one thing, over and over, and that is what they become in the listener's mind. A single story creates stereotypes, and the problem is not that they are false but that they are incomplete.
look.cite: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, The Danger of a Single Story, TED talk, 2009 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Adichie says stereotypes are incomplete rather than simply false. Give an example from this chapter where a true pattern could become a single story.

check.q: What is the difference between a generalization and a stereotype?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing
A generalization describes a pattern with evidence; a stereotype claims everyone in a group is alike
A generalization is always about one person
check.why: Generalizations describe patterns loosely with evidence; stereotypes turn patterns into fixed rules about everyone.

check.q: What did Adichie warn about in her 2009 talk?
choices: The danger of a single story about a people
The danger of learning too many languages
check.why: Her talk argued that a single story creates incomplete stereotypes.

check.q: Which sentence avoids a stereotype?
choices: Every Japanese family lives with grandparents
On average, Mexican households are larger than German households
check.why: It uses on average and states a measurable pattern instead of a claim about everyone.

review.q: Which country uses a dual system that pairs paid company work with vocational school?
review.why: Germany's dual system is its famous apprenticeship model.

review.q: Who created the world's first national social insurance in the 1880s?
review.why: Bismarck, Germany's conservative chancellor, created health, accident and pension insurance.

review.q: Which country has the highest share of people aged 65 and older in the chapter's data?
review.why: About 29 percent of Japan's people are 65 or older.

review.q: What is a conditional cash transfer, like Mexico's Progresa?
choices: A loan to build informal settlements
Money for poor families who meet conditions such as keeping children in school
review.why: Progresa paid families if children attended school and had health checkups.

review.q: How does Japan's government compare with Mexico's?
choices: Japan's parliament chooses the prime minister; Mexico's voters elect the president directly
Both are ruled by an emperor
review.why: Japan is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Mexico is a presidential federal republic.

review.q: What does the chapter say about religion in Japan?
choices: Most people say they have no religion but take part in shrine and temple rituals
review.why: Japanese religion is often about practice more than stated belief.

review.q: A student writes, All Mexicans live with their grandparents. What is the main problem?
choices: It turns a pattern into a stereotype about everyone
review.why: Words like all turn a pattern into a stereotype; many families differ.

review.q: Why is the World Values Survey a fairer tool than a traveler's impressions?
choices: It is written by government leaders
It asks people in many countries the same questions about their own values
review.why: The survey records how people describe their own values, using the same questions everywhere.
